title: Replace an Outlet or GFCI
summary: Swap a worn, loose or two-prong outlet for a new tamper-resistant outlet or a GFCI, wired correctly and tested.
safety: Turn the breaker off and prove the outlet is dead with a tester before touching any wire. Test the tester on a live outlet first. Never work with the power on.
pro: you find aluminum wiring, scorched or crumbling insulation, a hot or melted outlet, a box crammed with many cables, or the breaker keeps tripping. Adding new outlets or circuits usually needs a permit.

questions.label: How many cables come into the box?
questions.hint: Not sure yet? Pick one; you'll count them in step 5 and can change it.

steps.t: Check what you have and buy the right outlet
steps.idea: The new outlet must match the circuit, and some locations require a GFCI.
steps.b:
1. Read the old outlet: the amp rating (15 or 20) is stamped on the face or the metal strap. Buy the same rating.
  2. Is the outlet within 6 ft of a sink, in a bathroom, kitchen counter, laundry, garage, basement or outdoors? It needs GFCI protection.
  3. Buy tamper-resistant ("TR") outlets. They're required in homes when you replace one.
  4. Look at the slots: if the old outlet has only two slots and no round hole, there's probably no ground wire. A GFCI is the code-approved fix for that.
faq: Can I put a 20 amp outlet on a 15 amp circuit?
No. Match the old outlet, and never install a higher rating than the breaker.
What's the T-shaped slot on a 20 amp outlet?
It lets 20 amp plugs fit. Regular plugs still work in it.
Does it need to be AFCI too?

Many areas now require arc-fault (AFCI) protection when you replace outlets in bedrooms and living areas. That can come from an AFCI breaker already in the panel or an AFCI outlet. Ask your local building department.

steps.t: Turn off the power at the breaker
steps.idea: Kill the power to the outlet at the panel, and make sure nobody turns it back on.
steps.b:
1. Plug a lamp or radio into the outlet and turn it on.
  2. At the panel, flip the breaker labeled for that room fully to OFF.
  3. If the lamp is still on, turn that breaker back on and try the next one until the lamp goes off.
  4. Put tape over the breaker handle with a note: "Working on outlet. Don't touch."
  5. Check both halves of the outlet: sometimes the top and bottom are on different circuits.

steps.idea: Never trust a breaker label. Test before you touch.
steps.b:
1. Test your non-contact tester on an outlet you know is live. It should beep or light up.
  2. Hold its tip at the short slot of each half of the outlet you're replacing. No beep = no power.
  3. Plug the plug-in tester into both halves. No lights = no power.
  4. Test the pen on the live outlet again, to prove it still works.
steps.stop: If anything beeps or lights up, stop. Find the right breaker before going on.

steps.t: Take off the plate and pull the outlet out
steps.idea: Get the outlet out of the box without touching the wire ends.
steps.b:
1. Remove the cover plate screw(s) and the plate.
  2. Remove the two long screws at the top and bottom of the outlet.
  3. Hold the metal strap and pull the outlet straight out of the box, gently, so the wires come with it.
  4. Hold the non-contact tester near every wire in the box. Nothing should beep.
steps.stop: Silver-colored wires (not copper) or "AL" printed on the cable mean aluminum wiring. Don't replace the outlet yourself; it needs special parts and an electrician.

steps.idea: A photo of the old wiring is your map for the new one.
steps.b:
1. Take two photos from different angles before you loosen anything.
  2. Count the cables entering the box. One cable = 1 black, 1 white, 1 bare. Two cables = two of each.
  3. If there are two cables, put a piece of tape on each wire of one cable and mark it "A".
  4. Note any wires pushed into holes in the back of the outlet ("backstab") instead of under screws.
faq: There's a red wire too.
The outlet may be half switch-controlled. Note which screw it's on and keep the metal tab between the brass screws in the same state as the old outlet. If unsure, stop and ask an electrician.

steps.idea: Free the wires without damaging them.
steps.b:
1. Loosen each terminal screw and unhook the wire.
  2. Backstabbed wires: push a small flat screwdriver into the release slot next to the hole and pull the wire out. No slot? Cut the wire right at the outlet.
  3. Look at the copper ends. If they're nicked, darkened or brittle, cut them off and strip fresh: 3/4" of bare copper.
  4. You need at least 3" of wire sticking out of the box. Shorter? Add a pigtail (step in the next phase).

steps.idea: A GFCI must know which cable brings power from the panel.
steps.b:
1. Separate the two cables so no bare ends touch anything or each other. Spread the wires out of the box.
  2. Turn the breaker on. Keep hands away from the box.
  3. Hold the non-contact tester near each black wire. The one that beeps is the LINE (power in). Only one should beep.
  4. Turn the breaker off again and test again: nothing beeps.
  5. Tape-label that cable's black and white "LINE".
steps.stop: Leave the breaker on only as long as the test takes. Never touch bare wire while it's on.

steps.idea: Clean, correctly stripped hooks make tight, safe connections.
steps.b:
1. Strip 3/4" of insulation using the matching gauge hole on the stripper (14 for 15 amp, 12 for 20 amp, usually).
  2. With needle-nose pliers, bend each end into a U-shaped hook.
  3. Straighten the bare ground wire and hook it the same way.

steps.idea: One short wire to the outlet, joined to both cables, keeps power flowing to the next outlet.
steps.b:
1. Cut three 6" pieces of wire the same size as the house wire: black, white, bare/green.
  2. Hold the two black wires and one new black piece with the ends even. Twist on a wire nut clockwise until tight.
  3. Do the same with the whites, and with the grounds.
  4. Tug each wire. Nothing should pull out.
  5. The pigtails now go to the outlet like a single cable.
faq: Can't I just use both sets of screws?
Yes, an outlet has two brass and two silver screws for that. Pigtails are easier and keep power flowing even if the outlet fails.

steps.idea: Ground first, then neutral to silver, then hot to brass.
steps.b:
1. Ground: hook the bare wire clockwise around the green screw and tighten.
  2. Neutral: white wire clockwise around a silver screw. Tighten firmly.
  3. Hot: black wire clockwise around a brass screw, on the opposite side from the white. Tighten firmly.
  4. Tug each wire. None should move.
  5. Tighten any unused terminal screws so they don't stick out.

steps.idea: Power in goes to LINE. LOAD is only for protecting outlets further down the circuit.
steps.b:
1. Find the words LINE and LOAD on the back of the GFCI. LOAD is usually covered with yellow tape.
  2. Ground: bare wire to the green screw.
  3. LINE: the power-in white to the LINE silver terminal, the power-in black to the LINE brass terminal. Many GFCIs clamp a straight wire under a plate: insert the straight end and tighten.
  4. {{a.cables==='two'?'Second cable: to protect the outlets after this one, connect it to LOAD (white to silver, black to brass). Or pigtail it with the LINE wires so those outlets are not protected.':'Leave the tape on the LOAD terminals.'}}
  5. Tug every wire.
faq: Do I need LOAD?
Only if you want the GFCI to protect other outlets after it, like the rest of a bathroom circuit.

steps.idea: A GFCI makes an ungrounded outlet safe for people, but it must be labeled.
steps.b:
1. Connect the GFCI without a ground wire (leave the green screw empty).
  2. Stick the "No equipment ground" label on the wall plate.
  3. Outlets protected through its LOAD side also get "GFCI protected" and "No equipment ground" labels.
faq: Is that safe?
Yes for people. A GFCI cuts power when current leaks, ground wire or not. Some electronics prefer a real ground, which needs new wiring.

steps.t: Fold the wires in and mount the outlet
steps.idea: Fold the wires neatly so nothing loosens or gets pinched.
steps.b:
1. Fold the wires behind the outlet in an accordion (S) shape.
  2. Push the outlet straight in. Don't force it; GFCIs are bulky, so fold the wires tight to the back of the box.
  3. Screw the strap to the box until it's snug and straight. Don't crack the plastic.
  4. Attach the cover plate.

steps.idea: Prove the new outlet works and is wired correctly.
steps.b:
1. Remove the tape from the breaker and turn it on.
  2. Plug in the plug-in tester. Compare the lights to the chart printed on it; you want "correct".
  3. {{a.kind==='gfci'?'Press TEST on the GFCI: it clicks and the power goes off. Press RESET: power comes back. Do this monthly.':'Plug in a lamp to be sure both halves work.'}}
  4. If anything looks wrong, turn the breaker off and compare your wiring with the photo.
faq: The GFCI won't reset.
Usually LINE and LOAD are swapped, or there's no power. Turn the breaker off and check which cable is LINE.
Tester says "open ground".
No ground wire is connected. Fine only for a labeled GFCI; otherwise check the ground connection.
Tester says "hot/neutral reversed".
Black and white are swapped. Turn off power and switch them.

testHelp.b:
1. Turn it on (some have a button you hold).
  2. Touch the tip to the short slot of an outlet you know is live. It should beep or flash.
  3. Now hold it at the outlet or wire you're testing. Silence means no voltage detected.
  4. Test it on the live outlet again afterward. A dead battery gives a false "safe".

hookHelp.b:
1. Strip 3/4" of insulation using the right gauge hole.
  2. Grip the very end with needle-nose pliers and roll it into a U.
  3. Hook it around the screw so the open end points clockwise.
  4. Squeeze the hook closed around the screw, then tighten the screw firmly.

nut.title: Twist on a wire nut
nut.cap: No bare copper should show below the nut.

glossary: The black (sometimes red) wire that carries power from the panel.
The white wire that completes the circuit back to the panel.
The bare or green safety wire.
Ground-fault circuit interrupter: an outlet that cuts power in a fraction of a second if current leaks, for example through a person.
On a GFCI: LINE is power coming in, LOAD feeds and protects outlets further along.
A short wire joined to the house wires with a wire nut, so only one wire goes to the outlet.
Push-in holes on the back of cheap outlets. Screws make a more reliable connection.
Tamper-resistant: outlets with shutters that keep kids from pushing things into the slots.
